_schema: Room content. The renderer's trust boundary, enforced in room.js:
_plain: PLAIN TEXT, escaped on render: cards[].name, groups[].title, groups[].symbols[].n
_raw: RAW AUTHORED HTML, injected as-is: cards[].body, cards[].note, examples[].q, examples[].steps[], examples[].ans, groups[].symbols[].g
_rule: Anything moved between those two lists changes what the browser does with it. Plain fields must never contain markup; raw fields are trusted and must never hold anything a reader typed.

cards.name: What is in an atom
cards.body: Protons set the element, neutrons set the isotope, electrons set the chemistry.
cards.note: Atomic number = protons. Mass number = protons + neutrons.

cards.name: Ions
cards.body: Metals lose electrons to form cations (+); nonmetals gain them to form anions (−).

cards.name: Valence electrons
cards.body: The outer-shell electrons — the only ones that bond.
cards.note: For main-group elements, the group number gives the count.

cards.name: Electronegativity trend
cards.body: ↑ across a period · ↓ down a group
cards.note: Peaks at fluorine. It drives bond polarity.

cards.name: Ionization energy trend
cards.body: ↑ across a period · ↓ down a group
cards.note: Harder to remove an electron from a smaller, more tightly held atom.

cards.name: Atomic radius trend
cards.body: ↓ across a period · ↑ down a group
cards.note: More protons pull the same shell in tighter; a new shell pushes it out.

cards.name: Bond type from ΔEN
cards.body: ΔEN > ~1.7 ionic · 0.4–1.7 polar covalent · < 0.4 nonpolar covalent
cards.note: The cut-offs are guidelines, not laws — bonding is a spectrum.

cards.name: Ionic vs covalent
cards.body:
Ionic: metal + nonmetal, electrons transferred, forms a lattice.
Covalent: nonmetal + nonmetal, electrons shared, forms molecules.
cards.note: Metallic: a lattice of cations in a sea of shared electrons.

cards.name: Octet rule
cards.body: Atoms tend towards eight valence electrons.
cards.note: H and He want two; period 3 and beyond can exceed eight.

cards.name: Intermolecular forces
cards.body: London dispersion < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding < ion–dipole
cards.note: These set boiling point and solubility — not bond strength.

cards.name: Hydrogen bonding
cards.body: Needs H bonded directly to N, O or F.
cards.note: Why water boils so much higher than its size suggests.

examples.ans: Na⁺Cl⁻ — open the Periodic Table room to inspect Na & Cl

examples.q: Which is larger, Na or Na⁺?
steps: Na⁺ has lost its entire outer shell
Same nuclear charge pulling fewer electrons

examples.q: Rank F, O, N by electronegativity

steps: ΔEN = 0.96 — in the polar covalent range
examples.ans: polar covalent, with Cl the negative end

examples.q: Why does water boil higher than H₂S?
steps: Both are bent molecules of similar size
O is electronegative enough for hydrogen bonding; S is not
